title: Article 11 — Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law

content.overview: Article 11 provides that nothing in the foregoing provisions of Part II shall derogate from the power of Parliament to make any provision with respect to the acquisition and termination of citizenship and all other matters relating to citizenship.
content.glance: Parliament has full power to regulate acquisition, termination and all citizenship matters. Citizenship Act, 1955 is the principal statute.
content.study:
Article 11 is the residual and continuing legislative power over citizenship.

Effect: Articles 5–10 do not limit Parliament’s power to make law on:
- acquisition of citizenship;
- termination of citizenship;
- all other matters relating to citizenship.

Principal statute: Citizenship Act, 1955 (as amended), which provides for citizenship by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation; renunciation, termination and deprivation; and related statuses (including overseas citizen of India cardholder — OCI — which is not full citizenship).

Relationship: Articles 5–8 fixed the initial body of citizens at commencement; Article 9 disentitled voluntary foreign citizens; Article 10 continued those rights subject to parliamentary law; Article 11 is the ongoing source of legislative power.

Examination: always state that modern citizenship law is primarily statutory under Article 11; the constitutional articles are the commencement framework plus the enabling power.

sections.heading: Constitutional text
sections.body: Nothing in the foregoing provisions of this Part shall derogate from the power of Parliament to make any provision with respect to the acquisition and termination of citizenship and all other matters relating to citizenship.

sections.heading: Exam checkpoints
sections.body:
1. Article 11 is plenary for citizenship legislation.
2. Citizenship Act, 1955 is the main implementing statute.
3. Distinguish commencement citizenship (Arts 5–8) from statutory modes (birth, descent, registration, naturalisation under the Act).
4. OCI is not citizenship.

examples.title: Illustration — Statutory regulation
examples.body: Parliament amends the Citizenship Act to alter the conditions for citizenship by registration or naturalisation. The amendment is sustained by Article 11 and is not constrained by the commencement-specific rules in Articles 5–8.

misconceptions.trap: Articles 5–8 still govern how a person born today acquires Indian citizenship.
misconceptions.correction: Articles 5–8 fixed citizenship at commencement. Acquisition today is governed by the Citizenship Act, 1955 under Article 11.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Explain Article 11.
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Article 11 provides that nothing in Articles 5–10 shall derogate from Parliament’s power to make any provision with respect to the acquisition and termination of citizenship and all other matters relating to citizenship. The principal statute is the Citizenship Act, 1955. Modern acquisition (birth, descent, registration, naturalisation) and termination are statutory under this power.

examTips: Art 11 = Parliament’s plenary citizenship power; Citizenship Act 1955 is the working law.
content.migrationNote: QUAL remediation 2026-10-09: parliamentary power and Citizenship Act link clarified.

keyTakeaways: Art 11: Parliament regulates acquisition, termination and all citizenship matters.
Citizenship Act, 1955 is the principal statute.
